title: 21  Perea and Harer (2015): sliding windows, periodicity, and coefficients
text:
21.1 The published target
Can persistent homology distinguish the shape of an oscillation from the strength of its periodicity? Perea and Harer, Sliding Windows and Persistence: An Application of Topological Methods to Signal Analysis, published in Foundations of Computational Mathematics 15, 799–838 (2015), connects this question to the geometry of delay embeddings. A periodic signal becomes a closed curve in a higher-dimensional space, and its longest \(H_1\) bar measures how strongly that curve persists through the Vietoris–Rips filtration.
Here we reproduce the two explicitly specified signals in Section 6.3 and Figure 3 of arXiv:1307.6188v2. The distinctive result is that the coefficient field can change the answer even for an ordinary scalar periodic signal. Our computations recover that effect. They also expose a numerical disagreement with the published figure, which we keep visible rather than conceal by tuning parameters.
The paper gives
\[
g_1(t)=0.6\cos(t)+0.8\cos(2t),\qquad
g_2(t)=0.8\cos(t)+0.6\cos(2t).
\]
Both have period \(2\pi\) and the same total squared harmonic amplitude. Their difference is which harmonic dominates. The stated experiment uses
\[
M=4,\qquad \tau=\frac{2\pi}{5},\qquad
T=\left\{\frac{2\pi k}{150}:k=0,\ldots,150\right\}.
\]
A window has \(M+1=5\) coordinates,
\[
SW_{M,\tau}g(t)=\big(g(t),g(t+\tau),\ldots,g(t+M\tau)\big),
\]
and spans \(M\tau=8\pi/5\), or 0.8 of a period. Confusing \(M\) with the number of coordinates changes the experiment. So does replacing \(M\tau\) by a full period.
For every window \(x\), the authors subtract its coordinate mean and normalize its Euclidean length:
\[
C(x)=x-\frac{1}{5}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{5}x_j\right)\mathbf 1,
\qquad z=\frac{C(x)}{\|C(x)\|_2}.
\]
This is normalization within each window, not standardization of the five coordinates across the entire dataset. We then compute \(H_1\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb F_2\) and \(\mathbb F_3\), using the Euclidean Vietoris–Rips filtration. Its scale is the maximum edge length of a simplex, exactly the convention in Section 3 of the paper.
The source includes \(t=0\) and \(t=2\pi\). We retain both, giving 151 windows and 150 distinct phases. Their distance is below \(4\times10^{-16}\) in floating-point arithmetic. The periodically repeated endpoint is documented rather than silently discarded.

title: 21  Perea and Harer (2015): sliding windows, periodicity, and coefficients
section: 21.2 Recreate the signals and compute the diagrams
text:
21.2 Recreate the signals and compute the diagrams
The local stack supplies MetricSpaces, TDARipserer, TDAPersistenceDiagrams, and TDAplots. Columns of the following matrix are points:
using MetricSpaces, TDARipserer, TDAPersistenceDiagrams, TDAplots
using Statistics
import LinearAlgebra: norm

times = 2π .* collect(0:150) ./ 150
M, τ = 4, 2π / 5
signals = [t -> 0.6cos(t) + 0.8cos(2t),
           t -> 0.8cos(t) + 0.6cos(2t)]

function normalized_windows(f, times, M, τ)
    X = [f(t + j * τ) for j in 0:M, t in times]
    X .-= mean(X; dims=1)
    radii = sqrt.(sum(abs2, X; dims=1))
    minimum(radii) > 1e-12 || error("Constant window")
    return X ./ radii
end

F3 = ripserer(Rips(cloud; threshold=Inf); dim_max=1, modulus=3)

21.4 Check the geometry independently
At \(M=4\) and \(\tau=2\pi/5\), the normalized window cloud for
\[
g(t)=r_1\cos(t)+r_2\cos(2t),\qquad r_1^2+r_2^2=1,
\]
is isometric to the following explicit four-dimensional curve:
\[
\widetilde z(t)=
\big(r_1\cos t,r_1\sin t,r_2\cos2t,r_2\sin2t\big).
\]
This provides a strong check on the window construction without reducing its dimension by PCA or changing the distances:
r1, r2 = 0.6, 0.8
Z4 = permutedims(hcat(r1 .* cos.(times), r1 .* sin.(times),
                      r2 .* cos.(2 .* times), r2 .* sin.(2 .* times)))

D1 = [norm(Z[:, i] - Z[:, j]) for i in eachindex(times), j in eachindex(times)]
D2 = [norm(Z4[:, i] - Z4[:, j]) for i in eachindex(times), j in eachindex(times)]
maximum(abs, D1 - D2)
# 1.609823385706477e-15

H1_4d = ripserer(Rips(EuclideanSpace(Z4); threshold=Inf);
                dim_max=1, modulus=3)[2]
Bottleneck()(F3[2], H1_4d)
# 4.440892098500626e-16
For \(g_2\), the largest pairwise-distance discrepancy is \(1.39\times10^{-15}\), and the bottleneck discrepancy is also \(4.44\times10^{-16}\). The raw five-coordinate windows have constant radius \(\sqrt{5/2}\), as expected from the orthogonal harmonic decomposition. After normalization, their norms differ from one by at most \(2.22\times10^{-16}\).
Passing the directly computed distance matrix to Rips also recovers all four diagrams within numerical precision. In addition, crosscheck.jl obtains exactly the same principal bar endpoints using both alg=:cohomology and alg=:homology. These checks exercise different inputs and reduction modes inside TDARipserer; they do not constitute a comparison against an independent persistence implementation.
We also replace \(g_1\) by \(3.2g_1+7\). Centering removes the constant, and unit normalization removes the positive amplitude multiplier. The resulting \(H_1\) bottleneck distance is \(2.22\times10^{-16}\). Thus the contrast between the two signals is not a difference in units or offset.

21.4.1 Test the paper’s finite-sampling bound
Theorem 6.8 concerns a Fourier cutoff \(N\) and a prime coefficient field \(p>N\). Here the two signals are already trigonometric polynomials with \(N=2\), so \(p=3\) meets the hypothesis and \(p=2\) does not. For these amplitudes, the bound becomes
\[
mp(D)\geq\sqrt3\max(r_1,r_2)
-\delta\,2\sqrt2\sqrt{r_1^2+4r_2^2}.
\]
The sample phases have Hausdorff radius \(\pi/150\) on the circle; the script chooses \(\delta=(1+10^{-10})\pi/150\) to satisfy the theorem’s strict density inequality. The lower bounds are 1.284414 for \(g_1\) and 1.300206 for \(g_2\). Their computed \(\mathbb F_3\) maximum persistences exceed these bounds by 0.261605 and 0.250072.
The \(\mathbb F_2\) value for \(g_1\), 1.130047, is below the corresponding expression. This is not a counterexample to the theorem: its field hypothesis excludes that computation.

21.6 Sensitivity and controls
Our extensions vary the delay through 15 ratios of \(2\pi/5\), retaining \(M=4\), the original 151 sample times, and \(\mathbb F_3\). The normalized mixture scores do not have their global maximum at the published delay: \(g_1\) reaches 0.926034 at a window of 0.32 periods, and \(g_2\) reaches 0.896161 at 0.24 periods, compared with their published-window scores 0.892594 and 0.895053. The near-period window has a clear theoretical justification, but this finite experiment does not justify treating it as the unique optimum for every signal.
For the pure cosine, we separately retain the unnormalized ellipse geometry from Section 2.1, dividing all windows by the same factor \(\sqrt{5/2}\). Per-window unit normalization would remove that radial geometry. The squared axes are
\[
a_{\pm}^2=1\pm\frac{1}{5}
\left|\frac{\sin(5\tau)}{\sin\tau}\right|.
\]

title: 22  Cohen-Steiner et al. (2007): persistence stability
text:
22.1 The target
How much can a persistence diagram change when its input function changes? Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Harer’s Stability of Persistence Diagrams gives a precise bound. Here we check that bound numerically with the local TDARipserer and TDAPersistenceDiagrams packages.
The author-hosted PDF is the earlier SoCG 2005 conference version, despite its filename. The citation above identifies the 2007 journal article. Both identify the same bottleneck stability inequality.
For continuous tame functions on a fixed triangulable domain, the stability theorem bounds diagram distance by function distance:
\[
d_B(D_k(f),D_k(g))\leq\lVert f-g\rVert_\infty.
\]
The bottleneck metric matches diagram points to each other or to the diagonal and minimizes the largest matching cost. A finite interval of lifetime \(\ell\) can disappear into the diagonal at cost \(\ell/2\). Matching points by their order in an exported CSV would not compute this metric.
We use coefficients in \(\mathbb F_2\), as in the conference paper. Our domain is a fixed finite square grid, and our input is a vertex-valued cubical filtration. Every cell enters at the maximum value of its incident vertices. If corresponding vertex values differ by at most \(\epsilon\), corresponding cell values also differ by at most \(\epsilon\). Consequently \(K_f(t)\subseteq K_g(t+\epsilon)\) and \(K_g(t)\subseteq K_f(t+\epsilon)\) for every level \(t\). These inclusions give the filtration bound on the domain actually computed.
The norm below is measured on those 961 vertices, not estimated for an unsampled continuous surface. Changing the grid, the boundary conditions or the domain would require a different comparison.

22.6 What this establishes
This checks the local cubical-persistence and bottleneck implementations against a mathematical constraint, including essential intervals and a case with a known exact distance. The theorem bounds the largest matching cost; it does not promise that the number of short intervals remains fixed under perturbation.

title: 23  Summary and further reading
text:
23.1 What we can now calculate
We began with a cloud of observations and the question of its shape. The square showed how to turn distances into simplices, simplices into boundary matrices, and cycles modulo boundaries into homology classes. A filtration then let us follow these classes as the scale changed.
The computations added choices that the abstract definitions alone do not make: units, preprocessing, metric, coefficients, filtration, sample size, and cutoff. We compared Rips, alpha, and cubical inputs; learned to read finite and essential intervals; and used shared-grid vectorizations and diagram distances.
ToMATo follows density peaks through merges. Mapper builds overlapping groups from a filter and a local clustering rule. Ball Mapper builds a cover around landmarks. Their plots tell us about those constructions. Edges in a displayed graph do not automatically certify holes in the underlying space, and a graph layout is not a faithful geometric map.
The applications tested those distinctions. The Target benchmark exposed a clustering failure. The digit experiment separated training, validation, and test transformations and included a pixel baseline. Delay embeddings required attention to sampling and independence. Shape comparisons required common vectorization coordinates and a decision about geometric scale.
Finally, the uncertainty chapter separated a stability theorem, empirical sampling variation, and a test under a stated null model. A long interval is a lifetime; its scientific interpretation remains a question about the data.

title: 23  Summary and further reading
section: 23.2 A workflow worth carrying to your next dataset
text:
23.2 A workflow worth carrying to your next dataset

State the question and sampling units. What phenomenon would a component, loop, or cavity represent? Which observations are independent?
Choose and record the representation. Inspect missing values, duplicates, units, and outliers. Justify the metric and filtration rather than accepting their defaults silently.
Predict a small result. Use a synthetic control or a hand-calculable example. Check conventions, including edge length versus ball radius and foreground versus background.
Separate fitting from evaluation. Fit preprocessing and diagram vectorizers on training data, select parameters with validation data, and reuse the fitted transformations on test data.
Check sensitivity and alternatives. Vary sample size and scientifically plausible parameters. Compare with classical methods and, when inference is intended, a justified null model or confidence procedure.
Report what the result cannot distinguish. A diagram is a compressed summary. Different objects can have the same diagram, and different constructions on one dataset can answer different questions.

The six JuliaTDA packages used here are frozen with the book’s environment. The setup notes explain how to reproduce this edition and how to switch to development sources.

23.3 Further reading

23.3.1 Books and surveys
For algorithms and the underlying mathematics, read Computational Topology by Edelsbrunner and Harer (Edelsbrunner and Harer 2010) or Topology for Computing by Zomorodian (Zomorodian 2005). Topological Data Analysis with Applications is by Carlsson and Vejdemo-Johansson (Carlsson and Vejdemo-Johansson 2021).
Hatcher’s Algebraic Topology develops the homology theory beyond our finite-field examples (Hatcher 2002). Ghrist’s Elementary Applied Topology offers a visual route into applied topology (Ghrist 2014).
Carlsson’s Topology and Data (Carlsson 2009) and Ghrist’s Barcodes: The Persistent Topology of Data (Ghrist 2008) are survey papers, useful companions to a first pass through this book.

23.3.3 Topics beyond this book
One-parameter persistence is not the end of the story. Multiparameter persistence can track, for example, distance and density together; its invariants are more complicated than a single barcode. Zigzag persistence permits objects to be added and removed, useful for changing observations over time. Cohomology and circular coordinates can turn a persistent loop into a useful coordinate rather than only a lifetime.
For geometric shape analysis, the persistent homology transform compares many directional filtrations; this is a broader construction than our small family of image directions. For other computational budgets, witness and sparse complexes and approximation guarantees deserve study. Distance-to-measure filtrations address robustness using a different geometric construction, rather than expecting ordinary Rips persistence to ignore outliers.
Sheaves and cosheaves extend local-to-global reasoning, while differentiable topology brings topological summaries into optimization. These are directions for further study, not prerequisites for the examples we have worked through.
Go forth and find some holes in your data! Then ask why they are there.
